claim: Synchronous activation of striatal cholinergic interneurons is sufficient to drive dopamine release via axo-axonal stimulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in brain slices.
source: Experiments in brain slices clearly show that synchronous activation of striatal cholinergic interneurons is sufficient to drive dopamine release via axo-axonal stimulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on the mechanism of acetylcholine-evoked dopamine release in brain slices.

claim: Evidence for acetylcholine-evoked dopamine release in vivo has been less forthcoming.
source: However, evidence for this mechanism in vivo has been less forthcoming.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the literature, based on inference from available studies.

claim: Mohebi, Collins and Berke reported that optogenetic activation of striatal cholinergic interneurons with blue light evokes dopamine release measured with RdLight1 in awake behaving rats.
source: Mohebi, Collins and Berke recently reported that, in awake behaving rats, optogenetic activation of striatal cholinergic interneurons with blue light readily evokes dopamine release measured with the red fluorescent sensor RdLight1 (Mohebi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim cites a specific published study (Mohebi et al., 2023).

claim: Blue light alone alters the fluorescent properties of RdLight1 in a manner that may be misconstrued as phasic dopamine release.
source: Here, we show that blue light alone alters the fluorescent properties of RdLight1 in a manner that may be misconstrued as phasic dopamine release, and that this artefactual photoactivation can account for the effects attributed to cholinergic interneurons.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Artefactual photoactivation of RdLight1 can account for the effects attributed to cholinergic interneurons.
source: Here, we show that blue light alone alters the fluorescent properties of RdLight1 in a manner that may be misconstrued as phasic dopamine release, and that this artefactual photoactivation can account for the effects attributed to cholinergic interneurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing photoactivation effects.

claim: Measurements of dopamine using RdLight1 should be interpreted with caution when combined with optogenetics.
source: Our findings indicate that measurements of dopamine using the red-shifted fluorescent sensor RdLight1 should be interpreted with caution when combined with optogenetics.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings of photoactivation.

claim: The conditions under which acetylcholine-evoked dopamine release occurs in behaving animals remain unknown.
source: In light of this and other publications that did not observe large acetylcholine-evoked dopamine transients in vivo, the conditions under which such release occurs in behaving animals remain unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and review of the literature.

claim: Dopamine axons are sensitive to acetylcholine.
source: However, the axons of DA neurons do stand out in their sensitivity to acetylcholine (ACh), whose release from striatal cholinergic interneurons in brain slices is potent enough to trigger axonal action potentials and locally evoke DA release (i.e., independently of somatic spiking activity) via the activation of β2-containing nicotinic ACh receptors on DA axons (Cachope et al., 2012; Threlfell et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Mamaligas et al., 2016; Kramer et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Matityahu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Acetylcholine release from striatal cholinergic interneurons can trigger axonal action potentials and locally evoke dopamine release via activation of β2-containing nicotinic ACh receptors on dopamine axons in brain slices.
source: However, the axons of DA neurons do stand out in their sensitivity to acetylcholine (ACh), whose release from striatal cholinergic interneurons in brain slices is potent enough to trigger axonal action potentials and locally evoke DA release (i.e., independently of somatic spiking activity) via the activation of β2-containing nicotinic ACh receptors on DA axons (Cachope et al., 2012; Threlfell et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Mamaligas et al., 2016; Kramer et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Matityahu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Dopamine release in ventral striatum can increase even when the firing of dopamine neurons in the midbrain appears unchanged.
source: This mechanism was proposed to underlie observations that DA release in ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens, NAc) can increase even when the firing of DA neurons in the midbrain appears unchanged (Berke, 2018; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published observations.

claim: Direct evidence for acetylcholine-evoked striatal dopamine release in vivo remains limited.
source: However, direct evidence for ACh-evoked striatal DA release in vivo remains limited.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Cachope et al., 2012 presented an example recording showing that strong optogenetic activation of cholinergic interneurons for several seconds is accompanied by dopamine elevation in the NAc of a urethane-anesthetized mouse.
source: In their original report of ACh-evoked DA release, Cachope et al., 2012 presented an example recording whereby strong optogenetic activation of cholinergic interneurons for several seconds is accompanied by DA elevation in the NAc of a urethane-anesthetized mouse.
evidence: This claim cites a specific finding from a published study.

claim: The patterns of dopamine and acetylcholine release in various striatal locations in vivo are strongly correlated on sub-second time-scales in a manner consistent with acetylcholine-evoked dopamine release.
source: More recently, we and others showed in mice and rats that the patterns of DA and ACh release in various striatal locations in vivo are strongly correlated on sub-second time-scales in a manner that is consistent with ACh-evoked DA release (Howe et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Chantranupong et al., 2023; Krok et al., 2023; Mohebi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including the authors' own work.

claim: Strong changes in dopamine dynamics were not observed in the dorsal and lateral striatum of mice after molecular, pharmacological and optogenetic interference with acetylcholine signaling.
source: Yet, we were unable to observe strong changes in the dynamics of DA in the dorsal and lateral striatum of mice after molecular, pharmacological and optogenetic interference with ACh signaling (Chantranupong et al., 2023; Krok et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' own published work.

claim: mApple-based fluorescent sensors including RdLight1 and the GRAB-rDA series may exhibit photoactivation.
source: However, one concern with these experiments is that mApple-based fluorescent sensors – including RdLight1 and the GRAB-rDA series (Zhuo et al., 2024) – may exhibit photoactivation (also known as 'photoswitching' or 'photoconversion'), a process whereby mApple's red fluorescence changes in the presence of blue light (Shaner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on mApple properties.

claim: Photoactivation is a process whereby mApple's red fluorescence changes in the presence of blue light.
source: However, one concern with these experiments is that mApple-based fluorescent sensors – including RdLight1 and the GRAB-rDA series (Zhuo et al., 2024) – may exhibit photoactivation (also known as 'photoswitching' or 'photoconversion'), a process whereby mApple's red fluorescence changes in the presence of blue light (Shaner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on mApple.

claim: R-GECO family red Ca2+ indicators grow brighter independently of Ca2+ for hundreds of milliseconds following brief flashes of blue light.
source: This phenomenon is one of the main downsides of the R-GECO family of red Ca2+ indicators, which also use mApple and grow brighter independently of Ca2+ for hundreds of milliseconds following brief flashes of blue light, limiting their use with optogenetics (Akerboom et al., 2013; Dana et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on R-GECO indicators.

claim: Photoactivation effects of RdLight1 are negligible when expressed in cultured kidney cells and imaged using light-scanning confocal microscopy.
source: In the case of RdLight1, it was previously shown that photoactivation effects are negligible when expressed in cultured kidney cells and imaged using light-scanning confocal microscopy (Patriarchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original RdLight1 characterization study.

claim: Whether RdLight1 shows photoactivation in vivo under conditions routinely used in behavioral experiments has not been investigated.
source: Whether RdLight1 shows photoactivation in vivo under conditions routinely used in behavioral experiments (i.e., full-field fiber photometry and optogenetic stimulation) has not been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Blue light evokes RdLight1 fluorescence transients in the absence of an opsin.
source: Blue light evokes RdLight1 fluorescence transients in the absence of an opsin
evidence: This is a main finding of the study, supported by experimental data in wild-type mice.

claim: RdLight1 was virally expressed in the dorsolateral striatum or nucleus accumbens of wild-type mice.
source: the laboratory of N.X.T. virally expressed RdLight1 in either the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) or NAc of wild-type mice (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Under standard continuous illumination conditions, transient increases and decreases in red fluorescence consistent with established patterns of dopamine release were observed.
source: Under standard continuous illumination conditions (565 nm excitation light, 30–50 μW at the tip of the fiber), we observed transient increases and decreases in red fluorescence consistent with established patterns of DA release (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Chantranupong et al., 2023; Krok et al., 2023; Markowitz et al., 2023; Mohebi et al., 2024), including spontaneous fluctuations during immobility and large-amplitude reward-evoked responses (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to established literature, shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Delivering blue light pulses through the same fiber at powers typically used for optogenetic manipulations evoked distinct transients in RdLight1 fluorescence resembling dopamine release.
source: Delivering blue light pulses (4 ms-long) through the same fiber at powers typically used for optogenetic manipulations (9 mW at the tip of the patch cord) evoked distinct transients in RdLight1 fluorescence resembling DA release (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is a key experimental finding shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: In the NAc, blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients averaged 7.0 ± 0.1% ΔF/F in magnitude, peaked 115±4ms after light onset and decayed back to baseline within 1 s (τdecay: 422±21ms; N=8 mice).
source: In the NAc, these transients averaged 7.0 ± 0.1% ΔF/F in magnitude, peaked 115±4ms after light onset and decayed back to baseline within 1 s (τdecay: 422±21ms; N=8 mice).
evidence: This claim presents quantitative experimental data from the study.

claim: In the DLS, blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients were smaller (4.5 ± 0.2% ΔF/F) but showed similar kinetics (time from light onset to peak: 129±2ms; τdecay: 516±60ms; N=8 mice).
source: In the DLS, blue light-evoked transients were smaller (4.5 ± 0.2% ΔF/F) but showed similar kinetics (time from light onset to peak: 129±2ms; τdecay: 516±60ms; N=8 mice).
evidence: This claim presents quantitative experimental data from the study.

claim: Blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients scaled in magnitude with the duration and intensity of light pulses in both NAc and DLS.
source: In both regions, blue light-evoked transients scaled in magnitude with the duration (Figure 1G–H) and intensity of light pulses (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G-I.

claim: Comparable increases in RdLight1 fluorescence were observed in mice that expressed RdLight1 in the ventrolateral striatum.
source: In parallel experiments taking place in the laboratory of B.L.S., comparable increases in RdLight1 fluorescence were observed in N=3 mice that expressed RdLight1 in the ventrolateral striatum (VLS; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming their occurrence across a range of experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a second laboratory, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blue light-evoked delayed fluorescent signals are specific to RdLight1, as they are not observed in mice expressing tdTomato.
source: These delayed fluorescent signals are specific to RdLight1, as they are not observed in mice expressing the red fluorescent protein tdTomato (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (control experiment with tdTomato).

claim: Blue light-evoked RdLight1 fluorescence transients do not reflect dopamine release.
source: Blue light-evoked RdLight1 fluorescence transients do not reflect DA release
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Wild-type mice used in the study do not express blue light-gated opsins to drive dopamine release.
source: First, our wild-type mice do not express blue light-gated opsins to drive DA release and DA neurons are not thought to be intrinsically sensitive to blue light.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and established knowledge about dopamine neurons.

claim: Dopamine neurons are not thought to be intrinsically sensitive to blue light.
source: First, our wild-type mice do not express blue light-gated opsins to drive DA release and DA neurons are not thought to be intrinsically sensitive to blue light.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about dopamine neuron properties.

claim: Blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients show little trial-by-trial variability in their amplitudes and kinetics.
source: Second, blue light-evoked transients show little trial-by-trial variability in their amplitudes and kinetics (Figure 1G and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G and J.

claim: Blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients do not display short-term facilitation or depression under a variety of stimulation conditions.
source: Third, blue light-evoked transients do not display short-term facilitation or depression under a variety of stimulation conditions (Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), calling into question their synaptic origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reserpine is an irreversible antagonist of the transporter required for loading dopamine into synaptic vesicles.
source: Fourth, we repeated the above experiments in a subset of mice treated with reserpine, an irreversible antagonist of the transporter required for loading DA into synaptic vesicles (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacological action of reserpine.

claim: Spontaneous fluctuations in RdLight1 fluorescence vanished in both the DLS and NAc after reserpine treatment.
source: Under these conditions, spontaneous fluctuations in RdLight1 fluorescence vanished in both the DLS (N=4) and NAc (N=4), confirming the absence of activity-dependent DA release in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from reserpine-treated mice.

claim: Blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients did not disappear after reserpine treatment and grew in amplitude and duration in both DLS and NAc.
source: By contrast, blue light-evoked RdLight1 transients did not disappear and, if anything, grew in amplitude and duration in both DLS and NAc (Figure 1J and K), demonstrating that they do not reflect synaptic release of DA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1J and K.

claim: RdLight1 displays strong photoactivation following exposure to blue light under wide-field illumination conditions routinely used to monitor and manipulate neural activity in vivo.
source: Our results show that RdLight1 displays strong photoactivation following exposure to blue light under wide-field illumination conditions routinely used to monitor and manipulate neural activity in vivo.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: RdLight1 photoactivation manifests as a prolonged, dopamine-independent increase in RdLight1 fluorescence that outlasts the blue light pulse and slowly decays back to baseline over hundreds of milliseconds.
source: This photoactivation manifests as a prolonged, DA-independent increase in RdLight1 fluorescence that outlasts the blue light pulse and slowly decays back to baseline over hundreds of milliseconds, giving it the appearance of synaptically-released DA.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental findings about photoactivation characteristics.

claim: Under the recording conditions used, RdLight1 photoactivation remained detectable with as little as 0.3 mW blue light.
source: Under our recording conditions, photoactivation remained detectable with as little as 0.3 mW blue light (Figure 1I), indicating that RdLight1 fluorescence should be interpreted with caution when combined with blue light in a variety of experimental conditions, including dual-color imaging of green and red fluorophores.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The initial characterization of RdLight1 may have failed to reveal strong blue light-mediated photoactivation because it used laser-scanning microscopy.
source: It is possible that the initial characterization of RdLight1 failed to reveal strong blue light-mediated photoactivation as it used laser-scanning microscopy (Patriarchi et al., 2020), which Roger Tsien and colleagues found in their original characterization of mApple produced significantly less photoswitching compared to continuous wide-field illumination (Shaner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to published literature about imaging methods and mApple properties.

claim: Laser-scanning microscopy produces significantly less photoswitching of mApple compared to continuous wide-field illumination.
source: It is possible that the initial characterization of RdLight1 failed to reveal strong blue light-mediated photoactivation as it used laser-scanning microscopy (Patriarchi et al., 2020), which Roger Tsien and colleagues found in their original characterization of mApple produced significantly less photoswitching compared to continuous wide-field illumination (Shaner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on mApple characterization.

claim: The light-evoked RdLight1 responses reported in Figure 1 of Mohebi et al., 2023 likely reflect photoactivation effect.
source: Our findings call into question the nature of the RdLight1 fluorescent transients reported in Figure 1 of the study by Mohebi et al., 2023. Given the similarity of our recordings in terms of response magnitude, timing and dynamics over a variety of stimulation parameters, it is likely that the light-evoked RdLight1 responses reported reflect this photoactivation effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current experimental data with published results.

claim: 405 nm illumination has not been shown to be the isosbestic point for RdLight1.
source: Although the study used 405 nm illumination to control for changes in fluorophore properties independent of ligand binding (i.e., the so-called isosbestic point), this deep blue wavelength has not been shown to be the isosbestic point for RdLight1.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of published characterization of RdLight1's isosbestic point.

claim: The isosbestic point of commonly-used green dopamine sensors is more green-shifted (e.g. 440 nm).
source: Indeed, the isosbestic point of commonly-used green dopamine sensors is more green-shifted (e.g. 440 nm; Sun et al., 2020), stressing the need for sensors to be published along with their full excitation/emission spectra, and for experimenters to tailor illumination wavelengths to their specific sensor.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on green dopamine sensors.

claim: It remains to be determined whether illumination at isosbestic wavelengths can contribute to or modify photoactivation.
source: It also remains to be determined whether illumination at isosbestic wavelengths can contribute to or modify photoactivation.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: Additional experiments will be needed to determine conditions under which cholinergic interneurons locally evoke dopamine release in the striatum of behaving animals.
source: Moving forward, additional experiments will be needed to determine conditions under which cholinergic interneurons locally evoke DA release in the striatum of behaving animals.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the current findings.

claim: Experiments using RdLight1 should include controls to account for the effects of blue light alone.
source: If using RdLight1, experiments should include controls to account for the effects of blue light alone, such as expressing RdLight1 only (i.e., no opsin), RdLight1 and a fluorophore [e.g., green fluorescent protein (GFP)] or a mutated sensor that does not bind DA.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Blue light illumination power should be kept as low as possible in optogenetic experiments with RdLight1.
source: Blue light illumination power should be kept as low as possible.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Optogenetic experiments may be designed using GFP-based dopamine sensors in combination with red-shifted optogenetic actuators.
source: Alternatively, optogenetic experiments may be designed using GFP-based DA sensors such as dLight1 (Patriarchi et al., 2018) or GRAB-DA3 (Zhuo et al., 2024) in combination with red-shifted optogenetic actuators (Klapoetke et al., 2014; Marshel et al., 2019), although this configuration is not without caveats either, as continuous blue light illumination may cause opsin activation.
evidence: This is a recommendation with citations to relevant tools, along with a caveat.

claim: Continuous blue light illumination may cause opsin activation.
source: Alternatively, optogenetic experiments may be designed using GFP-based DA sensors such as dLight1 (Patriarchi et al., 2018) or GRAB-DA3 (Zhuo et al., 2024) in combination with red-shifted optogenetic actuators (Klapoetke et al., 2014; Marshel et al., 2019), although this configuration is not without caveats either, as continuous blue light illumination may cause opsin activation.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of optogenetic actuator properties.

claim: Photoactivation is not unique to RdLight1.
source: Importantly, photoactivation is not unique to RdLight1.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by knowledge of other fluorescent sensors.

claim: Other mApple-based sensors, including the GRAB-rDA and R-GenGAR-DA families of red dopamine sensors and the R-GECO family of Ca2+ indicators show photoactivation when presented with blue light.
source: Other mApple-based sensors, including the GRAB-rDA and R-GenGAR-DA families of red DA sensors (Sun et al., 2020; Nakamoto et al., 2021; Zhuo et al., 2024), as well as the R-GECO family of Ca2 +indicators (Akerboom et al., 2013; Dana et al., 2016) show photoactivation when presented with blue light, with individual constructs differing in the polarity, magnitude and duration of photoactivation effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on these sensors.

claim: Individual mApple-based constructs differ in the polarity, magnitude and duration of photoactivation effects.
source: Other mApple-based sensors, including the GRAB-rDA and R-GenGAR-DA families of red DA sensors (Sun et al., 2020; Nakamoto et al., 2021; Zhuo et al., 2024), as well as the R-GECO family of Ca2 +indicators (Akerboom et al., 2013; Dana et al., 2016) show photoactivation when presented with blue light, with individual constructs differing in the polarity, magnitude and duration of photoactivation effects.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from published literature about these sensors.

claim: Photoactivation extends beyond mApple, as many fluorophores can modify their biophysical properties when presented with different wavelengths of light.
source: Photoactivation also extends beyond mApple, as many fluorophores can modify their biophysical properties when presented with different wavelengths of light.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of fluorophore properties.

claim: Photoactivation is the biophysical principle on which some molecular tracking and super-resolution imaging methods are founded.
source: It is, for instance, the biophysical principle on which some molecular tracking and super-resolution imaging methods are founded (Lippincott-Schwartz and Patterson, 2009; Chozinski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on imaging methods.

claim: Experiments should be designed carefully to control for photoactivation and other potential confounds, particularly when novel sensors are introduced.
source: Experiments should therefore be designed carefully to control for these and other potential confounds, particularly when novel sensors are introduced.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings and general principles of experimental design.
